Name: Chuck Holbrook
Question: How come in San Francisco it is very common to find many men who are over the age of 30 who have never had a girlfriend despite trying, but in most places in the world it is not as difficult as in San Francisco?
Answer: It’s a sausage fest for one. There’s 40% more men then women in the 20 to 35 age bracket in the heart of San Francisco where all the jobs in the city are. The rest of the Bay Area doesn’t get much better either. It’s at its worst if you work in certain industries like tech. Not that you can’t meet women outside of work, but if the only woman you interact with on a regular basis is the token woman who has had to begrudgingly adapt to the brogrammer culture, there’s not a lot of opportunity to learn the finer points of conversing with the opposite sex and unfortunately for the Bay Area computer scientists women here have not yet come to appreciate a l33t speak T-shirt over flattery and small talk. The low 6 figure paychecks that accompany the tech jobs that anywhere else in the nation would make you a good provider doesn’t even get you close to middle class here. Living with a gaggle of male roommates well into your 30s, just to afford rent, also isn’t entirely conducive to dating either. To top that all off, relationships greatly enhance your chance of having kids, which makes living anywhere in the Bay Area for anyone who doesn’t have $1.5 million for a tiny starter home a non starter. San Francisco doesn’t just lack women, it also has less under 18 residents per capita then any other US city. A number of those male techies who do miraculously win at the mating game end up leaving the area along with their mate so their kids can have a comfortable home. That’s not to say there aren’t women in San Francisco or families or a lot of highly successful people beating the odds. I still know more 30 year olds who are in active relationships then not, but “not” is still a common thing. Being married or on a path to some serious relationship in your 30s is not the near universal thing it is in other cities I have known.

Question: If democrats campaign on repealing this year’s tax cut will liberals vote for them because they don’t want lower taxes?
Answer: I’m 25+ years away from retirement. I live in a high tax stake. I make a decent amount to be taxed at a high rate, but not nearly enough to see the windfalls the top 0.01% will see. The tax “cuts” give us a trillion dollar deficit at a time when we should be taking advantage of the economy to pay down debt, not finance luxuries for already profitable businesses. Social security is on a death spiral and we are on track to pay more then 50% of all descretianry spending to debt service. The tax cuts are not paid for. It is a loan the baby boomers have taken out and passed onto thier children. I will vote democratic because I want to pay less in taxes over my lifetime and avoid the costs of financial mismanagement. I want those trying to pass on thier debt so they can retire wealthy to pay thier fair share. I don’t care if taxes are high or low, what I want is value from how my money is spent. Taxes that get me good schools and a stable middle class lifestyle with robust support structures to support me is money well spent. The Republican tax plan robs the government I rely on of the revenue that’s needed to sustain middle class living and uses it to pay those gaming the system and not paying thier fair share. Many government entities are horribly bloated and need reform. Robbing them of money does not make them nimbler, it simply takes away all the good and leaves only the most disfunctional parts that are willing to cheat to stay afloat. I would vote Republican if thier policies were aimed at cutting costs by making government services more efficient, instead tax cuts are down without thought to whether the revenue was being spent efficiently or not. I will vote democratic because they know that tax cuts have the be paid for and the ones we just got are going to cost me way more over the next decadethen they are worth now.

Name: Chuck Holbrook
Question: As an early employee, I own a part of a startup that's about to IPO. These shares constitutes almost all of my wealth. As an aspiring conservative value investor of age 30, how much and at what rate should I sell off my shares after the IPO?
Answer: Sell all of it. There is one trick to being a good investor. It’s diversification. The current direction of the stock does not matter. Intrinsic value and every other metric that so-called experts tout is dwarfed by being properly diversified. Stop looking at charts and past performance, those are for different questions. Investment advice on what and when to trade is for help on which stocks you should invest the small fraction of your income on and you should have multiple stocks across a broad range of categories. Talk to an accountant who can help you figure the best way to minimize the tax implications when selling, that may effect when you want to sell, but you do want to sell and sell as soon as possible. If you still want to be invested in a risky new IPO stock after selling, buy similar stocks in similar categories with a small fraction of your assets. Unless you are an executive and can take advantage of some inside knowledge, there is no benefit to you being overly invested in your employer. Assuming you want to continue working there, you will continue to be defacto heavily invested in the company by your salary. Everything else should be sold and diversified.

Name: Chuck Holbrook
Question: Does academic study in software engineering (computer science) help us learn the tech (senior web/software developer) better and deeper?
Answer: Academic study gives us patterns to use with the hodgepodge of software frameworks. It’s certainly possible to build a successful app without that, it’s just nearly impossible to scale it. If you want other developers to understand your code. Heck, if you want to be able to miantain your code for more then a year after you wrote it, you need a plan to organize and build it. Thinking about how to build your software for the long term in a way that allows it to be built into anything anyone may think of in the future is extraordinarily difficult. Knowing how to classify the efficiency of your algorithms abstractly lets you build perform at software that will scale as your user base does. There are so many things you won’t discover with just coding experience. The output of Academic study is rarely intuitive or obvious, but ironically, knowing abstract academic concepts allows us to make really hard software problems into something that is intuitive and obvious to solve. Yes, the study of software engineering is absolutely necessary to understand software development at its deepest levels. Not knowing it won’t stop you from building great software, it will just make it a lot harder to do so.
